_comment: Per-finding gosec waivers for code outside Phase 0/Part 0 (W1-W6)/Phase 1 scope, per the Phase 0 CI harness item's pre-existing-findings policy (.SPECIFICATION/IMPLEMENTATION.md). Every entry names one exact (file, line, rule) finding gosec currently reports and a reason; it is not a blanket rule or directory exclusion. A finding that stops matching (because the surrounding code moved) must be re-reviewed, not silently re-added: that is deliberate, not a maintenance burden to route around. Every entry's backstop is AGENTS.md's actual rule, quoted in full: 'gosec and govulncheck must be validated prior to production packaging (Phase 20).' CORRECTED TWICE on 2026-08-15, and the second correction is the one that matters. This header used to assert that AGENTS.md required ZERO REMAINING WAIVERS before Phase 20. It does not, and never did; the sentence above is AGENTS.md's only rule on the subject and it says nothing about waiver counts. The zero-waiver bar was written into Phase 0's pre-existing-findings policy, copied into this header, and attributed in both places to AGENTS.md, so removing it is deleting a misquotation rather than a phase relaxing a project rule it was measured against. Both copies were struck on the same day; the Phase 0 one is the origin. UPDATED 2026-08-15 by Phase 20b, which is the entry that paid the promise off: the three insecure-cookie entries (G124, CookieCodec.writeInsecure, Handler.writeInsecurePreference, Handler.writeInsecurePreAuthCookie) are GONE, removed with the code they guarded rather than re-waived, because the controller now terminates TLS and refuses to serve plain HTTP unattended (cmd/controller's resolveTLS). Twelve entries became nine and the whole cookie class is closed. What the nine are: one G705 in internal/api/logs.go, three G710 open-redirect entries in internal/ui/web/auth.go (whose lines moved when the insecure writer was deleted from that file, so each was re-reviewed against unchanged code and renumbered, never silently re-added), three G101 heuristic matches on the word 'credential' in a scope name and a form-field prefix, one G101 on an AWX endpoint name, and one G204 in internal/testsupport's docker build helper. Seven of the nine name Phase 39 as re-verifier and Phase 39 has closed, so Phase 82 was appended to own them rather than leaving a stale pointer; two are test-only (tests/parity/awx.go, internal/testsupport/ansible_image.go) and guard no shipping artifact, which is machine-checkable and true even though gosec-check itself draws no such boundary. One caveat this file has always understated, re-measured on the same day: it is the SMALLER of two suppression channels. Inline '#nosec' comments account for 56 further suppressions that never appear here, which is gosec's own Stats.nosec under the exact command tools/gosec-check runs, so this file's nine entries are about 14 percent of the project's suppressed findings rather than all of them. That count went UP by one in Phase 20b even while three waivers were deleted: the container healthcheck reads its own TLS_CERT_FILE to verify the local listener, which is a G304 the same shape internal/crypto's key_resolve.go already carries, so the honest summary of that phase is three waivers and one class removed, one inline suppression added. Quote the 56 with its method, because it is fragile: 67 raw lines match a grep for the string, 56 are suppressions under this project's invocation, and 101 if -tests is added, which tools/gosec-check does not pass. The bar Phase 20 was held to was zero remaining waivers OF THE COOKIE CLASS, and it is met. Nothing here sets a project-wide zero-waiver deadline, because no phase owns one; if that bar is wanted it needs a phase behind it, not a sentence. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-16 by Phase 20f, the pass that narrowed internal/tlscert's ownership rule to the one thing it protects, and this measurement supersedes every one below it. Nine waivers, unchanged and unmoved: no guarded line shifted, so nothing needed re-review, and the nine are the same nine listed above. Zero G124. The inline count reads 58 under the exact command tools/gosec-check runs, up one from 57, and the one is this pass: internal/tlscert/read.go's existing G304 is unchanged, and the new suppression is in cmd/controller/servingcert_race_test.go, on the exec.Command that starts the long-lived child for TestARunningControllerSurvivesASiblingsRenewal. It is the same shape as the two that file already carries and the reason is the same one: the program is os.Executable() and the only argument is a fixed -test.run flag, so nothing in it comes from input. Two suppressions were AVOIDED rather than written and both are worth recording. The new private-key detection parses candidate DER through crypto/x509 rather than shelling out to openssl, so there is no G204 anywhere near the decision that protects a secret. And the refusal messages name the running user through os.Geteuid rather than reading /etc/passwd or an environment variable, so no file is opened to build an error string and no G304 arises on a path that only exists to be printed. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-15 by Phase 20e, the pass that replaced the certificate claim lock with a design that has no lock, and this measurement supersedes the ones below it. Nine waivers, unchanged and unmoved: no guarded line shifted, so nothing needed re-review, and the nine are the same nine listed above. Zero G124. The inline count still reads 57 under the exact command tools/gosec-check runs, and it is worth saying what did NOT change it, since this pass added three suppressions and removed three. Added: two G204 in cmd/controller's new servingcert_race_test.go and one more in internal/tlscert's concurrent_test.go, each on an exec.Command whose program is os.Executable() and whose only argument is a fixed -test.run flag, which is how both packages start real processes to race each other over one directory. Removed: the two that Phase 20d recorded as deliberately AVOIDED are gone along with the code that avoided them, and the sentence recording them is now history rather than description. There is no generation lock to be an os.Mkdir instead of an O_CREATE|O_EXCL open, and no retry schedule to be jittered with crypto/rand instead of math/rand, because there is no retry: a controller loads what is published, writes one file if it has to, and loads again. The NFS reasoning that chose mkdir is not lost, it is satisfied more cheaply, since rename(2) is atomic everywhere that matters and every write in internal/tlscert is now a rename of a file no other writer names. tools/devcert and tools/uidev moved from //go:build ignore to //go:build devtools in the same pass and are compiled and vetted by `make ci`; gosec is still run with no -tags, so neither is scanned and neither adds a finding, which is the same boundary the ignore tag drew and the reason the tag was kept rather than deleted. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-15 by Phase 20d, the adversarial-fix pass over 20b and 20c, and this is the measurement that supersedes the two below it. Nine waivers, unchanged and unmoved: no guarded line shifted, so nothing needed re-review, and the nine are the same nine listed above. Zero G124, which is the bar Phase 20 was actually held to. The inline count reads 57 under the exact command tools/gosec-check runs, up one from 56, and NONE of that one is this pass: internal/tlscert/read.go gained a G304 for reading certificate material through a guard that refuses anything which is not an ordinary file, and cmd/controller/healthcheck.go LOST the G304 20b added, because the probe no longer reads its own certificate file at all and asks internal/tlscert for its trust anchors instead. One in, one out, net zero. The 57th belongs to the Helm chart work landing alongside this one (tools/helm-lint/main.go's G204 on a fixed "helm" literal), so a later reader comparing counts should attribute it there rather than here. Two further suppressions were AVOIDED rather than written, and both are worth recording because the obvious implementation of each would have needed one. The generation lock several controllers contend for is an os.Mkdir rather than an os.OpenFile with O_CREATE|O_EXCL, which raises no G304 and is additionally the primitive that is unambiguous on the NFS-backed ReadWriteMany volumes this whole fix exists for. The jitter on the retry schedule is crypto/rand rather than math/rand, which raises no G404; it does not need to be unpredictable, only uneven, and the cost of the stronger source once at start-up is a syscall. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-15 by Phase 20c, which made TLS self-provisioning the default: nine waivers, unchanged and unmoved (no guarded line shifted, so nothing needed re-review), and the inline count is still 56. Zero new suppressions, which was not luck: the new internal/tlscert package writes through os.CreateTemp, whose 0600 mode is both what a private key wants and the reason no G306 is raised, and it validates a stored pair through tls.LoadX509KeyPair rather than os.ReadFile, so no G304 arises for the two files it reads back. The one G304 in cmd/controller/healthcheck.go is the SAME suppression Phase 20b added, with its comment reworded to say the path may now also be a self-provisioned certificate; it is not a second one.

waivers.reason: Owned by Phase 11 (API Gateway & Telemetry). This is the SSE stream's "event: init" write, which gosec traces jobID into from a chi URL parameter. Phase 11 closed the underlying risk rather than only waiving it: jobID is rejected unless it parses as a UUID (internal/api/logs.go's StreamLogs, the uuid.Parse guard near the top of the handler), so the value reaching this Fprintf can no longer contain a newline, an angle bracket, or any other character with meaning to an SSE consumer or a browser. The same check closed a real NATS subject-wildcard injection on the subscribe path (FAILURE_PATTERNS.md). gosec's taint analysis cannot see the guard, so the finding remains reported; it is not reachable. Re-reviewed 2026-08-11 (Phase 19): the waiver went stale because this line moved from 135 to 147 when the wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin above it was removed and replaced by a comment explaining why (FAILURE_PATTERNS.md #95). That staleness is the waiver file working as intended -- a finding whose surrounding code moved must be re-reviewed, not silently renumbered -- so the guard was re-read and confirmed present and unchanged before updating the line. The endpoint now also accepts a session cookie, which widens who can reach it but not what jobID may contain. Re-verify at Phase 39.

Owned by Phase 19 (Brutalist UI Scaffold). Handler.setSkin's redirect after recording a theme-family choice. gosec traces the Referer header into http.Redirect and cannot see that Handler.safeReturn constrains it. The underlying risk is closed rather than only re-waived: safeReturn discards rather than validates, parsing the Referer and keeping only its path, so scheme, host, userinfo and fragment are thrown away outright instead of being inspected for something that looks safe. What remains is path.Clean'd, resolving traversal, and then required to be the UI prefix or a path beneath it, so the return value is always a rooted path on this origin. internal/ui/web/safereturn_test.go proves it against 17 real open-redirect techniques including protocol-relative URLs, userinfo hosts, backslash normalisation, traversal, and prefix look-alikes such as /uiadmin. gosec found two genuine defects here before this waiver existed -- an unescaped caller-controlled id reaching path.Join, and an earlier substring-based safeReturn -- both fixed rather than waived. Re-verify at Phase 39. Re-reviewed 2026-08-14 (Phase 79b): the waiver went stale because this line moved when the sign-in handlers were extracted from this file into login.go and writeInsecurePreference's doc comment grew. That staleness is the waiver file working as intended, so the guarded code was re-read before the line was updated: safeReturn and writeInsecurePreference are both byte-identical to what the original review covered, and only their line numbers changed. Re-reviewed 2026-08-15 (Phase 20b): the waiver went stale because this line moved when the development-only insecure cookie writers were deleted from this file and from internal/ui/session, which is the fix Phase 20 was carrying for them rather than an unrelated edit. That staleness is the waiver file working as intended, so the guarded code was re-read before the line was updated: safeReturn and all three appearance handlers are byte-identical to what the original review covered (the diff for this file touches only writePreference's doc comment and the deleted writer), and only their line numbers changed. Re-reviewed 2026-09-13 (web UI page-anatomy work): this waiver went stale for two reasons at once, and both were re-read rather than having the line number bumped. The line moved by two because net/url and strings left this file's imports when safeReturn's body did. More importantly the guarded code is no longer byte-identical: the redirect target now comes from Handler.returnTo (internal/ui/web/preferences.go) rather than Handler.safeReturn, and returnTo reads a second caller-controlled source, the _return hidden form field, in preference to the Referer. The constraint itself is unchanged and is now in exactly one place, Handler.constrain, which safeReturn also delegates to: it still discards rather than validates, parsing the candidate and keeping only its path, so scheme, host, userinfo and fragment are thrown away outright instead of being inspected for something that looks safe. What remains is path.Clean'd, resolving traversal, and then required to be the UI prefix or a path beneath it, so the return value is always a rooted path on this origin. Two things were added on top: a 2048-byte cap, so an unbounded caller-supplied string cannot reach a response header, and a navigationParams allowlist, so the query string that now rides along carries only tab, after, limit and q rather than being echoed back. A query cannot change which origin a Location points at, which is why carrying one is safe; carrying only parsed parameters follows refreshURL's existing rule in the same package. The new form-field source has its own evidence rather than inheriting the Referer's: internal/ui/web/preferences_test.go's TestReturnTo_CannotBeRedirectedOffOrigin runs the same class of open-redirect techniques through the field, and internal/ui/web/safereturn_test.go's 17 cases still cover the Referer path unchanged.

Owned by P0 (the AWX parity corpus, .SPECIFICATION/AWX_PARITY_ROADMAP.md). This is the ObjectType constant CredentialTypes = "credential_types", the corpus's name for AWX's /api/v2/credential_types/ endpoint and its testdata subdirectory. G101 pattern-matches the substring "credential" in an identifier and a string literal and flags it as a possible hardcoded secret; there is no secret here, only a resource name this project did not choose (AWX's own). Renaming it would break the stated contract that ObjectType's value is literally the AWX endpoint's plural (this file's own ObjectType doc comment), for no security benefit. Re-verify if this constant's value ever changes to something gosec's heuristic was actually built to catch.

Owned by the template-kind-routing rebuild (FAILURE_PATTERNS.md #112, HANDOFF_ARCHIVE.md's "Phase 21 shipped, the template rebuild" entry), which moved this test-only image builder out of cmd/runner's release gate so tests/e2e could share it. BuildAnsibleRunnerImage runs `docker build -f <dockerfile> -t <tag> <root>`, and G204 flags dockerfile and root as caller-controlled variables reaching exec.Command. Neither is: dockerfile is this package's own repoRoot(tb) plus the fixed, repository-committed literal "Dockerfile.legacy-ansible-runner", and root is repoRoot(tb) itself, found by walking up from the test binary's own working directory until a go.mod is found, never from any external input. This is a testing.TB-gated helper (tb.Helper(), tb.Skip if docker is absent), unreachable from any production binary or network-facing path; gosec's taint analysis has no way to see that "variable" here means "computed by this process from its own module root," not "supplied by a caller."

Owned by Phase 22 (Credential Types & The Injector Engine). This is the ScopeCredentialRead constant, auth.Scope("credential:read"). G101 is a heuristic over identifier and literal text, and it fires here on the word "credential" appearing in both; there is no secret involved. The value is an authorization scope name, the exact string a JWT's "scopes" claim carries, and it is necessarily a compile-time constant for the same reason every other Scope in this file is: the vocabulary is closed, and a typo in a scope literal silently grants a scope nobody holds rather than failing to build. The eleven scopes above it are not flagged only because none of them happens to contain a word gosec's wordlist matches. Reviewed 2026-08-13: the constant holds no credential material and never will, since what it names is a permission to see that a credential EXISTS. There is no endpoint anywhere behind this scope that returns a secret value, which is enforced by internal/archtest's TestAPINeverImportsTheCredentialResolver rather than by review. Re-verify at Phase 39. MOVED AND RE-REVIEWED 2026-09-13: this finding sat at line 125 until ScopeSettingsRead and ScopeSettingsWrite were added above it in this file, which shifted it to 146. Nothing about the constant changed: same identifier, same literal, same closed vocabulary, same absence of secret material, and TestAPINeverImportsTheCredentialResolver still enforces that no endpoint behind this scope returns a secret value. So the reasoning above stands exactly as written and this is the renumbering of a re-reviewed finding, not a silent re-add, which is the distinction this file's header draws for the internal/ui/web/auth.go entries that moved the same way. MOVED AND RE-REVIEWED 2026-09-19: this finding sat at line 146 until ScopeRunbookCheck, the runbook:check scope that ScopeRunbookExecute implies, was added above it with its ten-line doc comment, shifting it to 156. Nothing about the constant changed: same identifier, same literal, same closed vocabulary, same absence of secret material, and TestAPINeverImportsTheCredentialResolver still enforces that no endpoint behind this scope returns a secret value. A renumbering of a re-reviewed finding, not a silent re-add. A renumbering of a re-reviewed finding, not a silent re-add.

Owned by Phase 22 (Credential Types & The Injector Engine). This is credentialPrefix, the string "credential_", which is a FORM CONTROL NAME PREFIX and not a credential. It namespaces the launch form's prompted credential inputs, so a control is named credential_<id>_<inputid> and cannot collide with a survey answer's answer_ control or with another bound credential's input of the same name; parseCredentialControl reads the same prefix back off the submission. gosec's G101 heuristic matches the identifier's name against a credential-shaped word list and cannot tell a prefix constant from a secret. There is no secret here to leak: the value is a literal that appears in rendered HTML on purpose, and the actual prompted values are read from the submission at request time and passed to LaunchTemplate as credtype.PromptedInputs, which recordConfig is structurally unable to see. Renaming the constant would silence the finding and would also break the deliberate symmetry with surveyPrefix directly above it in actions.go, which is the pairing that makes the two namespaces legible. Re-verify at Phase 39.

These are the NAMES of a credential's input fields, not values. The block declares InputUsername, InputPassword, InputPrivateKey and InputPassphrase as the strings "username", "password", "ssh_key_data" and "ssh_key_unlock", which are AWX's own input identifiers and what internal/credtype/managed/types/scm.json declares. G101 is a heuristic over identifier and literal text and it fires on the word "password" appearing in both; there is no secret here and there cannot be one, because what these name is a KEY into a map whose values live somewhere this package never reads. They are constants for the reason every other closed vocabulary in this codebase is: three places have to agree about them (the chooser that offers a credential, the check that refuses an unusable one, and the composition root that maps a resolved credential onto a project.Auth), and they were previously duplicated as string literals in the last of those with nothing keeping them in step. A typo in one copy silently produced an Auth with an empty password and a clone that failed to authenticate for no visible reason. Identical in kind to the two G101 entries on internal/auth/scopes.go above, which fire on the word "credential" in an authorization scope name for the same reason. Reviewed 2026-09-13. Keyed on an exact line: if the block moves, re-review it rather than renumbering on faith. MOVED AND RE-REVIEWED 2026-09-13: this sat at line 226 until AuthenticatesGit was keyed on the credential's kind, which added a credtype import above it and shifted the block by two. The constants are unchanged, character for character, and so is everything the reasoning above rests on: they are still map keys, still declared once so three callers cannot drift, and still hold no value of any kind. A renumbering of a re-reviewed finding, not a silent re-add. MOVED AND RE-REVIEWED 2026-09-15: this sat at line 228 until the asynchronous sync work added ErrSyncInProgress, an io import, the SyncRun type, Result.StartedAt and three Store methods above it, shifting the block by sixty-nine lines. The four constants are unchanged, character for character, and so is every premise the reasoning above rests on: they are still the NAMES of a credential's input fields, still map keys into values this package never reads, and still declared once so the chooser, the refusal check and the composition root cannot drift apart. Nothing about the sync work touched them or their callers. A renumbering of a re-reviewed finding, not a silent re-add. The four constants are unchanged, character for character, and every premise the reasoning above rests on still holds: they are the NAMES of a credential's input fields, keys into values this package never reads, declared once so the chooser, the refusal check and the composition root cannot drift apart. Nothing in the launchable work touched them or their callers. A renumbering of a re-reviewed finding, not a silent re-add. The four constants are unchanged, character for character, and every premise above still holds: they are the NAMES of a credential's input fields, keys into values this package never reads. Owned by the tools/sweep maintenance command, added 2026-09-15 (Makefile targets sweep, sweep-dry, sweep-timer, sweep-timer-off). tools/sweep is a developer-run command under tools/: it is package main, never linked into any cmd/ composition root, never reachable from a network path, and never packaged. Owned by Phase 78d (the certificate-presenting path). This is the SecretPFXBase64 constant, the string "pfx_base64", and it is the NAME of a key in wire.DispatchPayload.Secrets rather than a value. G101 is a heuristic over identifier and literal text: the identifier begins with "Secret" because every constant in this block does, and the literal ends in "base64" because the value that key addresses is base64. Neither is a credential and neither can become one, because what this names is a map key whose value is supplied at dispatch and never appears in this package at all. The four constants beside it (SecretUsername, SecretPassword, SecretPrivateKeyPEM, SecretPassphrase) have sat here since Phase 16 without firing, and SecretCertificatePEM landed in the same commit as this one and does not fire either, which is worth recording because it shows the rule is reacting to the "base64" token rather than to anything about how this constant is used. Identical in kind to the internal/project/project.go entry above, which is the same heuristic firing on the same thing (the names of a credential's input fields), and to the two internal/auth/scopes.go entries, which fire on the word "credential" in an authorization scope name. Renaming the constant to quiet the scanner was considered and rejected: the literal is a wire format that a Runner and a queued JetStream message already agree on, so it is not free to change, and choosing an identifier to satisfy a heuristic rather than to describe the thing is how a codebase ends up with names nobody can explain. Reviewed 2026-09-20. Keyed on an exact line: if the block moves, re-review it rather than renumbering on faith.

Owned by Phase 78d (the certificate-presenting path). This is certificateTransport.Transport's tls.Config, which sets MaxVersion to TLS 1.2 on the client-certificate path. gosec reads any MaxVersion below the current maximum as a weakening; here it is a workaround for a limitation in Go's own TLS stack, and it is the entire reason this transport exists rather than the library's. THE CAUSE IS THIS CLIENT, NOT THE TARGET, and the distinction is recorded because the first version of this waiver got it wrong and blamed Windows. TLS 1.3 removed renegotiation and replaced it with post-handshake authentication (RFC 8446 section 4.6.2), which is how http.sys asks for a client certificate once it knows the requested URL. Go's crypto/tls does not implement it: Conn.handlePostHandshakeMessage accepts a session ticket and a key update and answers anything else, a CertificateRequest included, with an unexpected_message alert. So the server asks, Go refuses, the server sees no certificate, and returns a bare 503. Over TLS 1.2 the same exchange happens by renegotiation, which Go does support. MEASURED BOTH WAYS on 2026-09-20 against Windows 11 build 26200: curl with TLS 1.3 FORCED and the same client certificate is answered 200, so the target is not the problem; Go over TLS 1.3 is answered 503, and the same Go call capped at 1.2 is answered 200. FAILURE_PATTERNS.md #275 records it in full. What the cap is and is not: MinVersion is ALSO TLS 1.2 in this same struct, so nothing below 1.2 can be negotiated and the window is exactly one version wide. TLS 1.2 with a modern cipher suite is not deprecated and is not the weakness gosec's heuristic is aimed at, which is a floor left at 1.0 or 1.1. It is scoped to the certificate path alone; password authentication goes through masterzen/winrm's NTLM and SPNEGO transports, which this file does not touch. Removing the cap would not make anything more secure, it would make certificate authentication stop working, and the practical effect is an operator falling back to NTLM password authentication, which is strictly worse than TLS 1.2 mutual authentication. One thing deliberately NOT waived beside it: InsecureSkipVerify is not set on this path at all, and Options.Insecure is REFUSED rather than honored, because presenting a client certificate to an unverified server hands it to whoever answers. TestTransportRefusesToSkipServerVerification holds that down. This waiver is EXPECTED TO BE PERMANENT, and that is a correction to its own first draft, which framed it as pending an upstream fix. Go's omission is deliberate: RFC 8740 forbids post-handshake authentication with HTTP/2 because it deadlocks multiplexed streams, and the Go team treats it as legacy complexity in the TLS state machine, holding that client authentication belongs in the initial handshake. They have said they are unlikely to implement it. So do not re-review this waiver expecting to retire it; re-review it if the tls.Config moves or if crypto/tls ever does ship PHA, in which case remove MaxVersion, delete TestTransportCapsTLSAtTwelve and prove the removal with the WinRM Release Gate against a real host. Reviewed 2026-09-20. Keyed on an exact line range: if the struct moves, re-review it rather than renumbering on faith. MOVED AND RE-REVIEWED 2026-09-20: this sat at 101-109, then 124-132, while the doc comment above it was rewritten twice: once to correct the cause (the first version blamed Windows; the limitation is Go's) and once to record that Go's omission is deliberate rather than pending. The tls.Config itself is unchanged character for character across both moves, and every premise above still holds: MinVersion is still TLS 1.2 so the window is one version wide, the cap is still scoped to the certificate path, and InsecureSkipVerify is still absent. A renumbering of a re-reviewed finding, not a silent re-add.

Owned by Phase 101c (mesh identity enforcement). This is the CredentialsEnv constant, the string "NATS_CREDS_FILE", and it is the NAME OF AN ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE rather than a credential or any part of one. G101 is a heuristic over identifier and literal text: the identifier begins with "Credentials" because the variable it names is where an operator puts the PATH to a credential file, and the literal contains "CREDS" for the same reason. Neither is a secret and neither can become one. The value this names is read by topology.CredentialsFromEnv, which takes the path, reads the file and returns its bytes to the caller; the constant itself is compiled into three binaries, a compose overlay and a Helm chart, all of which state it in plain text already because an operator has to set it. It exists as a constant precisely so those six copies cannot drift, which is the opposite of a hardcoded credential: a hardcoded credential is a value that should not be in source, and this is a name that must be identical everywhere it appears. Identical in kind to the internal/auth/scopes.go and pkg/wire/dispatch.go entries above.

Owned by Phase 118 (verification others can run), added 2026-09-30. tools/testgate is a developer and CI command under tools/: package main, never linked into any cmd/ composition root, never reachable from a network path, never packaged, the same boundary tools/sweep's G703 waivers rest on. This is summarize's os.OpenFile of the path in GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, which GitHub Actions sets for each step to the file that step's summary page is built from; gosec traces the environment variable into a filesystem path. The file is only ever opened for appending text this tool wrote, with O_APPEND|O_CREATE|O_WRONLY and mode 0o600, never read, executed or passed to a command.
